claims.text: HEA multilayer coatings have superior resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation because of coherent interfaces between distinct layers.
Coherent multilayer interfaces impede dislocation glide.
Coherent multilayer interfaces impede dislocation climb.
Interface-mediated obstruction increases the energy barrier for creep deformation at elevated temperature.
The proposed test material is a fully dense HEA coating with nanoscale layers and coherent, chemically distinct interfaces.
Creep deformation is prominent under sustained loading at 600–800 °C.
Adjacent HEA layers have lattice mismatch and distinct chemical ordering.
Engineered interfaces generate localized misfit stresses and enhanced lattice distortions.
Dislocation climb can govern elevated-temperature creep in an HEA.
Interface-induced stresses and distortions increase the activation energy for dislocation climb.
The interface barriers slow creep relative to homogeneous single-phase coatings.
Under identical high-temperature loading, multilayer coatings will have significantly lower creep strain rates than monolithic HEA coatings.
Multilayer coatings will show a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to monolithic HEA coatings.
The mechanism is effective only while layer thickness remains in the nanoscale regime.
Loss of interface coherence or interface quality diminishes the creep-resistance effect.
Overly thick layers diminish the creep-resistance effect.
The relative contributions of interfacial barriers and bulk HEA lattice resistance are not quantified.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or delayed dislocation movement relative to the monolithic control would falsify the interface-governed hypothesis.
